summary: A first-person incident report by a reporter describing a September 18, 2023 internet outage attributed to a coronal mass ejection (CME) inducing currents in undersea cables. It explains how geomagnetic storms can damage cable repeaters, how the outage disrupted work and personal life, and how recovery took a week of international effort. It closes with resilience measures such as redundancy, shielding research, and improved space weather monitoring.
one_line: A reporter recounts a September 2023 internet outage blamed on a solar CME affecting undersea cables, and the recovery and resilience efforts that followed.
key_facts: On September 18, 2023, the author lost internet connectivity in an outage attributed to a coronal mass ejection (CME).
A week before the outage, the Space Weather Prediction Center had issued alerts about potential geomagnetic storms from an unusually intense CME.
Dr. Emily Castor, a space weather physicist, describes CMEs as "massive bursts of solar wind, plasma, and magnetic fields rising above the solar corona or being released into space."
Sarah Patel, CEO of Global Connectivity Solutions, says undersea cables carry an estimated 99% of international data.
Geomagnetic currents generated during solar storms can induce voltage surges in long undersea cables.
Electrical engineer Dr. Alan Nguyen says induced currents can cause "substantial damage to the cables' repeaters," which amplify signals over long distances.
Dr. Jacob Torres, an astrophysicist, had mentioned that solar storms could affect satellite communications and power grids.
The outage caused missed deadlines and postponed interviews for the author, and affected sectors from financial services to healthcare, education and governance.
Technicians went to sea to locate and repair damaged cable segments while control centers rerouted data through less affected paths.
Full restoration took a week of effort and robust international cooperation.
Dr. Castor stresses building resilience through redundancy, shielding, and improved detection.
Sarah Patel's firm started exploring technologies to better withstand geomagnetic disturbances.
Research into shielding materials and meshed redundancy network architecture is underway to prevent total communications collapse.
Enhanced monitoring satellites now orbit closer to the Sun, relaying real-time data to improve space weather prediction.
